newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish parties seek to reinforce ailing peace.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish parties seek to reinforce ailing peace.

text.p: Northern Ireland's rival parties will hold crucial talks on Monday to try to buttress a peace process shattered by IRA bombs and a volatile Protestant Loyalist truce.

As hopes grew that pro-British guerrillas would keep alive a ceasefire jeopardised by Irish Republican Army violence, a senior Loyalist politician appealed to Catholic and Protestant parties to end old quarrels and give the divided community fresh hope.

David Ervine, a leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, the political arm of the banned Ulster Voluteer Force, said responsibility for breaking new ground lay with the major Protestant Unionist and Catholic Nationalist parties.
They must begin the process, he told Reuters, "of cutting a deal that will give the people of Northern Ireland a belief that politics can work and that peace is a viable option."

An IRA car bomb attack on Britain's military headquarters south of Belfast last week dealt a devastating blow to the province's peace hopes and raised the spectre of Loyalist retaliation and a sectarian war.

Leaders of the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), which controls outlawed Protestant groups, met secretly and some loyalists had expected a decision on Sunday on whether they would hold to a two-years-old truce or avenge the IRA attack.
Loyalist sources said that the absence of a public statement meant that the truce was still in operation but they were unsure how secure it was.
The uncertainty darkened an already clouded political drive for peace in multi-party talks chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchel that resume on Monday.
The talks, from which Sinn Fein is barred, have been stymied by wrangling over how to get guerrillas to disarm.
Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's Sinn Fein arm, said at the weekend that the region was "on the edge of an abyss". He called for unconditional all-party talks that would include his party.

But Britain and Ireland said an IRA bomb attack last week which killed a soldier and wounded 30 other people was a grim vindication of their decision to exclude Sinn Fein from talks until the IRA forsakes war.
The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February setting off bombs in mainland Britain. Last Monday's bombing was the first in more than two years in Northern Ireland.
Leaders of Unionist parties, speaking for most in the pro-British Protestant majority, say that neither security measures nor concessions are needed to combat IRA resurgence.

"You have to show that violence does not pay, quite the reverse, that the result of violence involves penalties and you are worse off as a result," David Trimble, head of the powerful Ulster Unionist Party said on BBC radio.
